overview: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a Dutch cloth merchant who made microscopes in Delft. Peering through a single tiny lens, he saw bacteria and other organisms too small for the unaided eye. His letters to the Royal Society in London helped establish the study of microscopic life.

keyMoments.title: A letter from Delft
keyMoments.text: The physician **Reinier de Graaf** urged his friend to share what he could see through his homemade microscopes. London’s **Royal Society** published Leeuwenhoek’s observations of mould, bees and lice in its journal. It was the beginning of a correspondence that lasted half a century, with Leeuwenhoek writing to London in his everyday Dutch.

keyMoments.title: Witnesses at the lens
keyMoments.text: In a letter to London, Leeuwenhoek described **tiny creatures moving in water**. The account strained even his readers’ growing trust in his lenses. **Witnesses in Delft** looked for themselves and attested to what they saw, giving the Royal Society testimony from people who had put their own eyes to the instrument.

keyMoments.title: A fellow across the water
keyMoments.text: The London physician **William Croone** nominated the Delft merchant for membership in the Royal Society. In February the society elected him **a fellow**, an honour Leeuwenhoek welcomed from home. He never attended a meeting in London, and his letters continued to carry his observations across the North Sea.

deepFacts.text: A Delft court record links the microscope maker to the painter **Johannes Vermeer**. On 30 September 1676 the city magistrates appointed Leeuwenhoek to administer the estate and assets of Vermeer’s widow, **Catharina Bolnes**. Among the tasks that fell to the man studying life in a drop of water was settling the household’s debts.

When **Peter the Great** visited the Netherlands in 1697, Leeuwenhoek went aboard the tsar’s boat with an unusual gift. His **eel viewer** let Peter examine blood flowing through a living eel, a sight the tsar could now reproduce with an instrument of his own.

connections.reason: Delft magistrates appointed Leeuwenhoek to administer the Vermeer household’s insolvent estate after the painter died.
Leeuwenhoek gave the visiting tsar an instrument for viewing blood circulation in a living eel.
